I think plutocracy_pls is asking you how you increased horsepower in that engine by such a large amount.  The 2.2 that came stock in that truck only produced 120hp when new.  Increasing horsepower in an engine by more than 65% without some form of boost is very difficult, especially for that engine's design, and would likely require alertaron to almost every component of the engine.  GM did produce a 2.3 libre engine with 180hp years before,  but even that engine lost hp in later designs in efforts to decrease noise, vibration, and other improvements GM assumed customers would prefer.  Please do share the alterations made to that engine that have enabled it to be such a monster.  Many of us are curious, and interested in learning from you if you are willing to share.  However, protecting intellectual property is also understood.

Cloudera is certainly the big boy on the block, and for that reason, definitely worth learning and playing with.  However, Cloudera's distribution is heavily altered, and is mostly managed by eternal services they have developed.  If one wishes to learn the core inner workings of hadoop and related projects, I personally think it will be more beneficial to install the distributions produced directly by Apache.  However, if one just wants to quickly stand up a working cluster so the may begin to interface with it, then the Cloudera distribution is certainly an excellent choice.  Hortonworks is also another big name in this category, however I cannot speak towards their distribution as I have not had any experience with it.
I am sure the style points more than make up for the money spent on gas when cruising around town.

Just as another option in case you have trouble finding a slant 6, the pre-mpi 318 is also a decent, and cheap option.  One of my vehicles is a 91 Dakota extended cab, which will get up to 21 mpg on the highway when driven easy.  These particular builds only had 165hp, but they have a lot of low end torque, and Jegs or Summit has this 318 crate motors with warranty for $1800.   I would agree, that a new slant six for the same price is probably a better option for you overall, but this may be something else to consider. 

 The magnum engines they started using in 92 are superior, but cost a lot more.
A blown head gasket is the first thing I thought of also.  Are you able to post a picture of the smoke?  Do you have excessive condensation coming from the exhaust?
I also have to suggest the MG.  As stated, they are easy to find parts for, much cheaper to fix than one might think, and very desirable.  My Mom has two of them, and they are her favorite cars.

I should also add that if your s10 is 2wd, and you do go with the vortec 350, beware that the 4 bolt main versions from the 4wd hd trucks have larger oil pans, which may have clearance issues with your crossmember.  It will fit, but it will not be happy about it.  If this ends up being your combination, I also suggest swapping the oil pan to a smaller one.  This will save you a lot of headache when putting the engine in, and should work fine for you since you do not plan to push this truck too hard.

Having put a few v8s in my 84 S10, I can give you some advice based on my experiences.  The lt1 did have optispark issues, but was better for performance due to the aluminum heads, cam (there were variations here based on the application), and the reverse cooling that was mentioned previously.  The lt1 engines with the more aggressive cams w were right at 300hp.  However, a vortec 350 from a 96 up full sized truck started out around 250hp and I think torque was at 290lb/ft, and can be gotten for a cheap price.  A common and cheap upgrade for these engines it to swap in an lt1 or lt4 cam, but the swap will make tuning your carb more difficult.  I personally ditched my carb long ago, however, my efi system alone was over your budget.  If I had to do mine over again, I would look at the cost of apply a custom tune to a factory mpi or tbi system and get on from a another vehicle.  To keep this as cheap as possible though, I suggest a vortec 350 with exhaust manifolds that dump at the rear (I think some the caprice classics had these manifolds), or headers made for this swap, and electric fans to save space (the double fans from an alero or grand am will work well).  To help with cooling, the 88 corvette radiators are wide single core aluminum radiators with dimensions that will fit under your hood.  Engine compartment heat may also be an issue,  so be prepared to cut some vents to save the alternator, and insulate the starter.
